paragraphs.text: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth. It covers about nine million square kilometers, almost the size of the United States, and in many places it gets less rain in a year than London gets in a week. From orbit it looks like a single orange sea of sand and rock.

stat.label: Area of the Sahara, the largest hot desert

shots.photo: File:Sand dune in the desert, Sahara Desert, Egypt.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Dunes in Egypt's Western Desert
The Sahara in Algeria, from the space station

paragraphs.text: In fact only about a quarter of it is sand. The rest is gravel plains, bare rock plateaus and mountains. In the Tibesti, in northern Chad, the volcano Emi Koussi rises to three thousand four hundred and fifteen meters, the highest point in the Sahara.

shots.on_screen_text: Sand seas of the central Sahara
Gravel plains of the eastern Sahara
Emi Koussi, Tibesti, Chad

paragraphs.text: But about ten thousand years ago, this was not a desert. There were lakes here, some of them enormous. There were rivers, grassland and trees. Hippos and crocodiles lived in the middle of what is now sand. People fished with bone harpoons, herded cattle and painted the animals they saw on the rocks. One of those lakes was about the size of the Caspian Sea.

shots.on_screen_text: The Ounianga lakes, northern Chad

shots.photo: File:Human Fingerprints on an Ancient Landscape (153611 - libya plateau oli2 20241117 lrg).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Dry river channels on a Libyan plateau
Rock art at Archei, Ennedi, Chad

shots.photo: File:Cave painting from the Tassili n'Ajjer mountains.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Cattle painting, Tassili n'Ajjer, Algeria

paragraphs.text: So what happened? How does a land of lakes turn into the biggest hot desert on the planet, and why did it happen so fast? The answer has to do with a slow wobble of the whole Earth. And what the green Sahara left behind is still feeding a rainforest on the other side of the Atlantic today.

shots.on_screen_text: Erg Chebbi dunes at sunrise, Morocco
The Tassili and the Erg of central Algeria

ask.text: Why did the Sahara turn to desert?

paragraphs.text: The first clues were painted on the rocks. In October 1933 a Hungarian explorer, László Almásy, found a rock shelter at the Gilf Kebir, a remote plateau in southwestern Egypt. On its walls were small human figures with their arms and legs spread, as if swimming. He called it the Cave of Swimmers. Decades later, Almásy and his cave inspired the novel and the film The English Patient.

stat.label: László Almásy finds the Cave of Swimmers, Gilf Kebir

shots.on_screen_text: The Gilf Kebir plateau
Cliffs and wadis of the Gilf Kebir
Egypt's Western Desert today
A wadi in the Gilf Kebir

stat.label: The English Patient: novel by Michael Ondaatje, then the film

paragraphs.text: Almásy believed the swimmers were real: that people had once swum in water here, in one of the driest places on Earth. Not everyone agrees on what the figures mean. But the paintings, thousands of years old, are only one site among many. In 2002 a small expedition found a second shelter a few kilometers away, now called the Cave of Beasts. Its walls hold thousands of painted figures: people, cattle, giraffes, ostriches, and strange headless creatures that gave the cave its name.

shots.on_screen_text: The Gilf Kebir, now among the driest places on Earth

paragraphs.text: Far to the west, on the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau in Algeria, there are more than fifteen thousand rock paintings and engravings, spread over about seventy-two thousand square kilometers. They were made over thousands of years. The oldest show wild animals: elephants, giraffes, rhinos and hippos. Later ones show herds of cattle, with people milking and driving them. Last come horses, and finally camels. You can read the drying of the Sahara on these walls, animal by animal.

stat.label: Rock paintings and engravings at Tassili n'Ajjer (UNESCO)

stat.label: The order of animals on the Tassili walls

paragraphs.text: Some of those animals never quite left. In the Ennedi mountains of Chad, at a gorge called the Guelta d'Archei, there is a pool that holds water all year. Camels come to drink there. And in that pool live a handful of crocodiles, perhaps fewer than ten. They have been cut off from every other crocodile for thousands of years, ever since the rivers that once linked the Ennedi to the rest of Africa dried up.

shots.photo: File:The Ennedi Massif in Northern Chad (iss072e404551).jpg

paragraphs.text: Then there are the bones. In the year 2000 a team led by the paleontologist Paul Sereno was looking for dinosaurs in the Ténéré desert of Niger. Instead they found a graveyard. At a place called Gobero, on the shore of a lake that has long since vanished, they excavated about two hundred human burials. Around the graves lay the bones of animals the people had eaten: hippos, crocodiles, turtles and big fish.

stat.label: Paul Sereno's team finds the Gobero graveyard, Niger

shots.on_screen_text: The Ténéré desert, Niger
The Ténéré near Gobero

stat.label: Burials excavated at Gobero, 2005-2006

shots.on_screen_text: Dunes over the old Gobero shore

stat.label: Animal bones found at Gobero

paragraphs.text: The first people buried there were hunters and fishers. They were tall and strongly built, and they were buried with harpoons and fishhooks made of bone. Next to them lay the bones of Nile perch, fish up to almost two meters long. Later came a different people, who also fished but kept cattle. One grave held a woman lying with two small children, their arms reaching toward each other.

shots.on_screen_text: Dry ground of the former Gobero lake

stat.label: The first fishers settle at Gobero

shots.on_screen_text: The Ténéré today
Dunes of the southern Ténéré

stat.label: A woman buried with two children, Gobero

paragraphs.text: And there are the rivers. Across the eastern Sahara, satellite radar and images show old river channels under the sand. One of them, the Wadi Howar, runs from the border of Chad toward the Nile. Geologists call it the Yellow Nile. For thousands of years it carried water, and herders and their cattle lived along it. Along its banks, archaeologists have found pottery, grinding stones and the bones of cattle. Today it gets at most a few centimeters of rain in a year.

shots.photo: File:Human Fingerprints on an Ancient Landscape (153611 - libya plateau oli2 20241117 lrg).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Fossil drainage on a Libyan plateau, Landsat 2024
Wadi Howar, Sudan
Along the dry Wadi Howar
Banks of the Wadi Howar

stat.label: Rain a year in the Wadi Howar today

paragraphs.text: The biggest of all the lakes was in the middle of the Sahara, in what is now Chad. Geologists call it Lake Mega-Chad. Its old shorelines, beach ridges and sand spits can still be traced across the desert. At its largest, around ten thousand years ago, it covered something like three hundred and forty thousand square kilometers, and in places it was more than a hundred and fifty meters deep.

shots.on_screen_text: Old shores of Mega-Chad, northern Chad

stat.source: Bouchette et al., Quaternary Research 2010; and others

shots.on_screen_text: The floor of Mega-Chad, central Chad

stat.source: Bouchette et al., Quaternary Research 2010; and others

paragraphs.text: In 2006 two geologists, Nick Drake and Charlie Bristow, used satellite images and radar height data from the Space Shuttle to follow those shorelines around the basin. They found beach terraces standing at almost exactly the same height, about three hundred and twenty-nine meters above sea level, hundreds of kilometers apart. A lake leaves a level line. These were its marks.

stat.label: Drake and Bristow map Mega-Chad's shorelines with Landsat and Shuttle radar

shots.on_screen_text: A beach ridge of Mega-Chad

stat.label: Height of a Mega-Chad beach terrace above sea level

shots.on_screen_text: Shoreline ridges at the northern edge of the old lake
Ridges on the old lake floor

paragraphs.text: That is about the size of the Caspian Sea, the largest lake on Earth today. Our map shows its shape, drawn from the height of the land: every low point that connects to today's Lake Chad, up to about three hundred and twenty meters above sea level. The lake filled a basin bigger than Germany.

chart.title: Lake Mega-Chad against today's lakes
chart.source: Bouchette et al., Quaternary Research 2010; and others; Wikipedia

stat.label: Our Mega-Chad outline: land below 320 m joined to Lake Chad (NOAA ETOPO)

paragraphs.text: From around eleven and a half thousand years ago until about five thousand years ago, Mega-Chad stood high. Then it shrank. Today's Lake Chad is what is left, a shallow lake on the southern edge of the Sahara. On average it is only about a meter and a half deep, full of reeds and islands. Tens of millions of people in Chad, Niger, Nigeria and Cameroon depend on its water and its fish. And even that is in trouble. Since the 1960s it has lost about ninety percent of its open water, to drought and to farming that takes water from its rivers.

stat.label: Years ago: Mega-Chad's long highstand

shots.on_screen_text: The northern basin of Mega-Chad
Lake Chad today

paragraphs.text: A few lakes survive far inside the desert. At Ounianga in northern Chad, about eighteen lakes sit among the dunes, fed not by rain but by water rising from under the ground, water that fell during wetter times. Some are fresh, some are saltier than the sea, and some are tinted red and green by algae. In 2012 UNESCO listed them as a World Heritage site.

A lake shore at Ounianga Serir

stat.label: The Lakes of Ounianga become a World Heritage site

paragraphs.text: North of the lake lies the floor of the old sea. The Bodélé Depression, in the low heart of the basin, was once under deep water. Today it is the dustiest place on Earth. It is covered in pale dust made partly of the shells of diatoms, tiny algae that lived in Mega-Chad, and of the bones of its fish. When the winds blow between the Tibesti and Ennedi mountains, they lift that old lake bed into the sky. From space, it is one of the easiest dust sources on Earth to spot: in winter, long pale plumes stream out of it toward the southwest.

shots.on_screen_text: The Bodélé Depression, the old lake floor

stat.label: The Bodélé: the largest single source of dust on Earth

shots.on_screen_text: Pale diatomite of the Bodélé

paragraphs.text: So why was the Sahara green? The answer is in the sky. Earth's axis is tilted, and it slowly wobbles, like a spinning top, tracing a circle about once every twenty-six thousand years. Together with the slow change in the shape of Earth's orbit, this wobble decides whether the north gets its summer when Earth is closest to the Sun or when it is farthest away. Today it is the second case: Earth is farthest from the Sun in early July, in the middle of the northern summer. That cycle comes back roughly every twenty-one thousand years. In the early twentieth century a Serbian engineer, Milutin Milanković, worked out these cycles by hand and argued that they drive the ice ages. He was right, and they drive the monsoons too.

stat.label: The slow wobble of Earth's axis, like a spinning top
One full turn of Earth's axis

shots.on_screen_text: The Sahel and Sahara from the space station

stat.label: When Earth is farthest from the Sun today
How often the northern summer sun peaks
Milutin Milanković calculated Earth's orbital cycles by hand

paragraphs.text: About ten thousand years ago, northern summers came when Earth was near the Sun. The summer sun over North Africa was several percent stronger than today. The land heated up more, and hot air rising over the Sahara drew in moist air from the Atlantic, like a sea breeze the size of a continent. The West African monsoon, which today brings summer rain only to the Sahel, pushed its rains hundreds of kilometers further north.

stat.label: Northern summer sunshine at the green/dry switch, compared with today (about)
stat.source: deMenocal et al. 2000; Shanahan et al. 2015

shots.on_screen_text: The Hoggar and Aïr region in summer

routes.label: Today the rains stop near the Sahel

shots.on_screen_text: The Gulf of Guinea coast, Côte d'Ivoire
The Sahel in Niger, end of the rainy season

paragraphs.text: And once the rains came, the land helped them. Grass and trees are darker than sand, so they soak up more sunlight. Plants breathe out water. Lakes add moisture to the air. All of that pulls in more rain, which grows more plants. The green Sahara kept itself green, until the push from the sky grew too weak. Scientists read this history in mud: pollen in old lake beds, and the dust and plant wax that washed into the sea off West Africa.

shots.on_screen_text: Fields and bush in the Sahel, Niger
Green and bare ground, Sahel
Rainforest around Lake Bosumtwi, Ghana
Lake Chad's wetlands
The central Sahara from orbit
Mud flats at the edge of Lake Chad
The Mauritanian coast, where Saharan dust meets the sea

paragraphs.text: This was not a one-time event. In 2023 a team of climate scientists modeled North Africa over the last eight hundred thousand years and found green periods roughly every twenty-one thousand years, each driven by the wobble. They were weaker or missing during the big ice ages, when ice sheets in the north held the rains back. At the height of the last ice age the Sahara was even bigger than it is today. Sediments under the Mediterranean and the Atlantic record the same rhythm, back for millions of years. The Sahara has been greening and drying again and again, like a slow heartbeat.

shots.on_screen_text: The Tademaït plateau, Algeria

stat.label: North African humid periods modeled over the last 800,000 years
Years between green Saharas, driven by precession

shots.on_screen_text: Saharan dust settling on the Atlantic

paragraphs.text: Those green windows may have mattered for our own species. Some researchers think that when the Sahara turned green, it opened corridors of water and grass across North Africa, and that groups of early humans used them to move north, toward the Mediterranean and beyond. When the desert came back, the doors closed again.

stat.label: Green periods may have opened routes north for early humans

shots.photo: File:ISS-64 Tassili N'Ajjer National Park, Illizi, Algeria.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Tassili n'Ajjer, on the route north
The Murzuq sand sea, Libya

paragraphs.text: Lake Mega-Chad went first in the north. As the rains failed, its level dropped, its northern arm toward the Bodélé dried out, and the great lake broke up into smaller ones. By about five thousand years ago, the floor of the northern basin was open to the wind.

shots.on_screen_text: The dry northern arm of Mega-Chad
The Bodélé, open to the wind

paragraphs.text: After about ten thousand years ago the wobble moved on, and the summer sun over North Africa slowly weakened. The monsoon began to retreat south. But how fast did the green disappear? In 2000 a team studying mud from the sea floor off Mauritania found a surprise. The dust in their core jumped suddenly, around five and a half thousand years ago. By their reading, the end of the green Sahara came within decades to centuries, not slowly over thousands of years.

routes.label: Today the rains stop near the Sahel

shots.on_screen_text: Cap Blanc, Mauritania, on the dusty Atlantic coast

stat.label: Sudden rise of Saharan dust in a core off Mauritania
How fast the end came, by the 2000 study

paragraphs.text: How can a slow wobble cause a fast collapse? Because the feedbacks run in reverse. As the rain weakened, plants died back, the land grew paler and reflected more sunlight, and the air over it stopped rising as strongly. Less rain meant fewer plants, and fewer plants meant less rain. Past a tipping point, the green could not hold itself up.

shots.on_screen_text: The southern Sahara in Mali, where the green ended
Thin vegetation at the Sahara's edge, Niger

shots.photo: File:Sand dune in the desert, Sahara Desert, Egypt.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Desert sand, Egypt

stat.label: Plants and rain feed each other, so a slow push can end in a fast fall
stat.source: deMenocal et al. 2000; Shanahan et al. 2015

paragraphs.text: Later studies made the picture more complicated. A 2015 study that brought together records from all over Africa found that the end came at different times in different places. At about twenty degrees north it came around five thousand years ago. Much further south, at Lake Bosumtwi in Ghana, the wet period lasted until about three thousand years ago. The rains did not switch off. They retreated south, and each place dried in its turn. They are still fragile today. In the 1970s and 1980s a long run of droughts brought famine to the Sahel, and Lake Chad shrank to a fraction of its size.

stat.label: Shanahan et al.: the end came later the further south
End of the wet period near 20° N

shots.on_screen_text: The dry northern basin of Lake Chad

paragraphs.text: The animals went the same way. Hippos, elephants and giraffes followed the water south, or died out. The herders' cattle needed grass, and the grass was going. Much later, in roughly the time of the Roman Empire, a new animal spread across the desert, one that could go for days without water: the camel. It is the last animal painted on the Tassili walls.

shots.on_screen_text: Savanna on the Niger-Nigeria border, where the herds went
Grazing land in the Sahel, Chad

stat.label: Camels become common in the Sahara, Roman era

shots.on_screen_text: The Tassili plateau today

paragraphs.text: For the people of the Sahara, that was enough. In 2006 two German archaeologists, Rudolph Kuper and Stefan Kröpelin, brought together radiocarbon dates from a hundred and fifty excavations across the eastern Sahara. They found people living across the region during the wet period, and then a sharp break in the Egyptian Sahara around 5300 BC. The herders left. One of the places they left behind is Nabta Playa, a dry lake bed in southern Egypt, where people set up a circle of standing stones about seven thousand years ago. Some researchers think it marked the summer solstice and the coming of the rains, though that reading is debated.

stat.label: Excavations behind the eastern Sahara timeline

paragraphs.text: Some moved south with the rains, into the Sahel. Many went east, to the one place in that region that still had water all year: the valley of the Nile. As the desert emptied, the Nile valley filled with farmers and herders. Kuper and Kröpelin argued that this crowding into a narrow river valley helped set the stage for the rise of pharaonic Egypt. The pyramids of Giza were built about two and a half thousand years later.

paragraphs.text: The green Sahara left more than paintings. Every year the winds lift dust off the Sahara and carry it across the Atlantic. A 2015 NASA study used a satellite laser to measure it. About twenty-seven million tons of that dust fall on the Amazon rainforest every year. Much of it comes from the Bodélé, the floor of Lake Mega-Chad. Some of the dust blows north instead, and every few years it turns the skies over Spain and the Alps orange.

paragraphs.text: That dust carries phosphorus, from the old lake's fish and algae. Amazon soils are poor in phosphorus, and rain keeps washing it away. The study estimated that about twenty-two thousand tons of phosphorus arrive from Africa each year, close to what the rainforest loses. A dead lake in the Sahara helps feed the largest rainforest on Earth.

stat.label: A nutrient the Amazon is short of
stat.source: Yu et al., Geophysical Research Letters 2015

paragraphs.text: The green Sahara also left water under the sand. Beneath Egypt, Libya, Sudan and Chad lies one of the largest groundwater systems in the world, the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer. Much of its water fell as rain during wet periods thousands to hundreds of thousands of years ago, and very little is being added today. In the Egyptian desert, farms pump that ancient water into green circles in the sand.

stat.label: Area of the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer
Much of it thousands to hundreds of thousands of years old

paragraphs.text: At the southern edge of the desert, people are trying to hold the line. In 2007 the African Union launched the Great Green Wall, a plan to restore a belt of trees, grass and farmland about eight thousand kilometers long, from Senegal to Djibouti. Progress has been slow and patchy. But in places, farmers who protect the trees that sprout on their fields have turned bare ground green again.

stat.label: The African Union launches the Great Green Wall

paragraphs.text: Will the Sahara turn green again by itself? If the wobble keeps its rhythm, the next peak of northern summer sun comes in about ten thousand years. How green the next green Sahara becomes may depend on how much greenhouse gas is in the air by then. And in 2018 one study suggested a shortcut: in a computer model, covering the Sahara with huge wind and solar farms more than doubled its rainfall, because the panels and turbines change how the land heats and the wind blows. Nobody has tried it at that scale.

stat.label: Until the next peak of northern summer sun

paragraphs.text: So the next time you see the Sahara on a map, remember that it has not always been this way. Ten thousand years ago it held a lake the size of the Caspian, rivers that ran toward the Nile, hippos and fishers and herds of cattle. A slow wobble of the Earth brought the rain, and a slow wobble took it away. The paintings, the bones, the crocodiles of Archei and the dust over the Atlantic are what is left. And the next time a dust storm turns a European sky orange, some of that dust may once have been the bottom of a lake. Five thousand years is a blink for a planet. The people who painted cattle on the rocks of the Sahara lived not long before the first pharaohs.

paragraphs.text: Here is my question for you. If you could visit the green Sahara for one day, ten thousand years ago, where would you go: fishing on Lake Mega-Chad, along the Yellow Nile with the herders, or to the painters at Tassili?

youtube.title: When the Sahara Was Green
youtube.description: About ten thousand years ago the Sahara was not a desert. It had lakes, one of them the size of the Caspian Sea, rivers flowing toward the Nile, hippos, crocodiles, fishers and cattle herders. This video follows the clues in the rock art, the graves and the dry riverbeds, explains how a slow wobble of the Earth brought the monsoon rains north and then took them away, and shows what the green Sahara left behind: dust that feeds the Amazon and ancient water under the sand.
